subject: Canada's economy stalled in July. Rates may still rise
bodyMarkdown:
Canada's economy did not grow at all in July, and the Bank of Canada may raise rates anyway four weeks from now. If you have a variable mortgage or a renewal coming, those two facts belong together.

## What actually moved in July

Statistics Canada reported on Tuesday that real GDP was essentially unchanged in July, a flat 0.0 per cent, after three straight months of growth and a second quarter that ran at a 3.3 per cent annualized pace. The mix underneath is the interesting part. Construction rose 1.3 per cent, its fourth straight monthly gain. Utilities rose 1.7 per cent on electricity generation, the sector's strongest month all year, which StatCan tied to the July heat wave. So the two things holding the number at zero were building and air conditioning. Manufacturing fell 0.9 per cent, its first decline in four months. Potash mining dropped 6.4 per cent, the biggest monthly fall since September 2025, on lower Saskatchewan output and weaker exports. Oil and gas extraction, retail and wholesale trade all slipped too. StatCan's **advance estimate**, an early read built from partial data, puts August back up 0.2 per cent, and that figure gets revised.

## The Bank of Canada's problem

Here is the squeeze. The Bank has held at 2.25 per cent since October 2025, seven decisions in a row, most recently on September 2. Growth just went to zero, which normally argues for cutting. But headline inflation is back at 3.0 per cent, the top of the Bank's control range, with gasoline up 25.7 per cent from a year ago on high global energy prices. You cannot cut into that. The Globe and Mail reported last week that swap markets had the October 28 decision at roughly 62 per cent hold and 38 per cent hike, close to a coin flip after a year of nothing happening. Claire Fan at RBC put it plainly: "If there's one thing that's really causing the pricing of the October meeting … it's oil prices." Derek Holt at Scotiabank says a hike is in play. Capital Economics has a hold as its base case, and calls it close.

## What potash and factories are telling us

I keep coming back to the potash line. A 6.4 per cent drop in a single month, tied to weaker exports, is what a trade fight looks like in the data instead of in a press conference. Manufacturing giving back its first month in four reads the same way. The Bank flagged on September 2 that new US tariffs and Canadian counter-measures, announced after trade talks broke down, make the growth picture harder to read. That is now showing up in the sectors that sell abroad, while the domestic ones (construction, utilities) carry the average. An economy that grows only where it is sheltered from trade is a narrower economy. A narrower economy is far more sensitive to whatever the Bank decides on October 28.

## The takeaway

Put October 28 in your calendar, because the Bank publishes a fresh Monetary Policy Report the same morning, which is where the whole forecast gets rewritten. If you are on a variable rate, work out today what an extra quarter point does to your payment, while it is still hypothetical. Watch the August GDP print when it lands next month, since that 0.2 per cent is an early estimate and it moves. And if you work in anything export-facing, treat the potash and manufacturing numbers as the earliest read you will get on tariffs, well ahead of any quarterly report.
